column3: God's making and rivers flowing beneath gardens echo provision from below, though the setting is eschatological.
Provision from above and beneath the feet is a remote spatial counterpart to the stream beneath Mary.
A call for water across the Fire and Garden contrasts sharply with Mary's immediate consoling provision.
Rivers flowing beneath everlasting gardens give a broader positive image of water supplied from below.
The messenger's immediately preceding announcement identifies the Lord who now reassures Mary.
God's direct call to Abraham parallels the responsive divine address, but the situation differs.
Garden rivers beneath the blessed are only a broad water-from-below parallel.
The immediate sequel continues Mary's physical relief with dates after the stream is provided.
Its garden rivers repeat a distant reward image rather than Mary's crisis provision.
Calling one's assembly is a public challenge, not the consoling call addressed to Mary.
The mention of what lies beneath the soil supplies only a lexical spatial parallel.
Fire above and below is an inverse image of the safe, life-giving source beneath Mary.
A mother facing danger is told not to fear or grieve and is promised divine restoration.
Mary's earlier question exposes the bewilderment that makes the later reassurance necessary.
Rivers beneath gardens retain only the general image of divine water provision.
Rivers beneath the saved and their grateful speech join water-from-below with a received call, but in Paradise.
The immediate sequel completes the reassurance: Mary is told to eat, drink, and have a comforted eye.
The promise that the godfearing will not grieve generalizes the relief given directly to Mary.
Garden rivers and good provision are a distant outcome parallel to Mary's concrete sustenance.
The prayer for coolness of the eyes only lightly anticipates Mary's commanded comfort of eye.
The night passing has no material connection to Mary's call, grief, or stream.
Unexpected provision from God clarifies the trustful source of Mary's unanticipated sustenance.
Mary's labor pain and wish for death immediately set up the command not to grieve.
The broad promise of no fear or grief lacks the maternal crisis and supplied provision of this scene.
Angels tell the steadfast not to fear or grieve and bring good news, closely paralleling divine reassurance.
The Lord's declaration that the birth is easy and merciful directly grounds the care given in 19:24.
Night travel under pursuit has no close link to Mary's stationary childbirth scene.
God's forgiveness and punishment describe the Lord generally but do not illuminate the reassurance.
Gardens and springs present a positive water-source image that broadly parallels the stream beneath Mary.
Hearing a caller and answering with prayer gives a related call-and-response pattern, though collective and devotional.
Zakariyya's private call to his Lord offers a same-surah model of a needy human addressed by God.
Mary's withdrawal while pregnant is the immediate narrative step before her labor and consolation.
Punishment from above or beneath the feet is a negative spatial contrast to the saving stream below.
Zakariyya's speech restriction only anticipates the later silence instruction to Mary, not 19:24 itself.
Jesus' later proclamation of shared lordship does not clarify the childbirth reassurance.
Moses being called by name shares the direct-address motif but not the maternal consolation.
Moses is assured not to fear during escape, a related pattern of divine reassurance in danger.
A secure station for the godfearing offers only general safety imagery.
The public call to prayer is unrelated to the private call that consoles Mary.
Angelic messengers reassure Lot and direct a nighttime escape, a related rescue-address pattern.
The opening of Mary's withdrawal narrative supplies the longer setting for her isolated childbirth.
Lot is told not to fear or grieve while rescue is promised, closely matching reassurance amid acute danger.
Stars for navigation do not materially illuminate Mary's grief or the stream beneath her.
Gardens and springs provide only a broad favorable water image.
The Day of mutual calling is an eschatological use of calling, not a consoling address.
Its account of formation in mothers' wombs gives relevant embodied context for Mary's miraculous pregnancy.
The later disagreement of factions does not bear on Mary's immediate consolation.
Putting deceivers underfoot is a hostile positional reversal, not the life-giving beneathness of 19:24.
The gathering and judgment of jinn and humans has no close relation to the scene.
Pharaoh's wife calls Moses a comfort of the eye, echoing the comfort promised Mary in the next ayah.
The general promise of no fear or grief lacks the scene's direct personal reassurance.
The use of make in a trial context does not clarify divine provision for Mary.
The introduction of the Lord's mercy to Zakariyya supplies only broad same-surah theological background.
Punishment from above and below is an inverse spatial image to Mary's protective provision below.
The command not to be grieved gives a direct verbal parallel, though addressed to the Prophet in another context.
Moses' mother is restored so that her eye is comforted and she does not grieve, a close maternal counterpart.
The divine address removing fear and grief extends the same assurance in an eschatological setting.
The order for Moses to depart at night does not clarify the childbirth consolation.
The later statement of an unavoidable decree shares Lord-language but no operative link to this ayah.
The promise of no fear or grief is a broad reward formula rather than situational comfort.
Tears of grief from lacking means form a limited contrast to Mary's sudden provision.
Gentle speech when material help is unavailable offers a related ethic of mercy and promised provision.
Calling from behind private rooms is a distant and improper form of address, unlike Mary's consoling call.
The no-fear-no-grief promise is a general afterlife assurance with little scene-specific overlap.
Zakariyya's request for an heir has no direct link to Mary's immediate relief.
Rivers beneath gardens are a distant reward image of sustained divine provision.
The question about the Elephant's companions has no relevant thematic connection.
Tranquility bestowed under a tree is only a loose spatial and consolatory parallel.
No fear or grief follows charitable giving, but the legal-reward setting is remote.
Pharaoh's summoning is a coercive public call, contrasting with Mary's merciful address.
The Lord's sovereignty over heaven, earth, and between them grounds the capacity to provide in Mary's isolation.
The command not to grieve, joined to God-given patience, gives a direct but less specific reassurance parallel.
Clear light sent from the Lord gives only broad divine-guidance background.
Noah's call to his Lord while overwhelmed parallels a distressed person receiving divine intervention.
No fear or grief in the reward for charity is a generic assurance formula.
Human striving toward the Lord does not illuminate the call, grief, or stream.
The assurance that the Lord does not forget gives distant same-surah support for divine attentiveness.
The marital sense of under does not relate to the stream beneath Mary.
The question about mountains has no material relation to the scene.
The Creator of earth and high heavens provides only a broad spatial-theological background.
Unheeded cries and calls are a negative contrast to Mary's effective, intelligible address.
Springs bursting from the earth give a concrete water-from-below parallel to the stream provided for Mary.
A pleasant drink in Paradise has no meaningful link beyond generic liquid imagery.
Noah's call and God's excellent response provide a general pattern of answered distress.
Zakariyya's direct call to the Lord is a close same-surah pattern of need met by divine mercy.
Jacob directs his grief to God, offering a close counterpart to grief held within a God-centered relationship.
Earth receiving revelation does not materially illuminate Mary's reassurance.
Garden rivers appear in a repentance-and-reward setting, distant from Mary's immediate provision.
A flowing spring is a concrete but eschatological water-source parallel.
It identifies grief as a burden and directs believers to rely on God, contrasting its malicious source with divine comfort.
God's making the Quran Arabic has no close relation beyond the verb make.
God reviving dead earth offers a broad life-restoring theme but no direct link to the scene.
The exception for worshippers has no material connection to Mary's consolation.
The reminder of earlier rejected messengers gives only general solace amid hardship.
Rules for private conversation do not relate to the call or provision in 19:24.
Remembering by one who fears does not clarify the ayah's imagery or situation.
Divine power over death and preserved food and drink only broadly supports miraculous provision.
Household conduct rules do not materially illuminate Mary's isolated childbirth.
Water relieving ritual difficulty offers a limited material parallel to water as merciful provision.
The comparison of those who strive and remain behind has no relevant connection.
The foundational promise that the divinely guided need neither fear nor grieve generalizes the assurance given to Mary.
Mary's unexpected provision in the sanctuary is the closest parallel of God directly sustaining her in seclusion.
The angels' choosing and purification of Mary supplies the immediate theological frame for her exceptional care.
The angelic announcement of Jesus to Mary closely parallels the annunciation that culminates in 19:24.
Jesus speaking in the cradle supports the later narrative evidence that the newborn may speak, relevant to the caller's identity.
The Quranic reference to the grave slander against Mary contextualizes the social crisis that follows her childbirth.
The command not to weaken or grieve offers a direct but nonspecific verbal reassurance parallel.
The Prophet is told not to be grieved by disbelief, a related divine command to resist sorrow.
God acknowledges that rejection grieves the Prophet, clarifying grief as a burden met by divine knowledge and support.
The direct command not to grieve because God is with the distressed recipient closely parallels Mary's reassurance.
The no-fear-no-grief formula gives a broad doctrinal counterpart without the maternal or provisioning setting.
Noah is told not to grieve over wrongdoing after divine judgment is disclosed, a parallel command amid distress.
The command not to despair of God's mercy reinforces the hope-bearing force of Mary's consolation.
Hearts finding rest in remembrance of God gives a theological counterpart to the command that calms Mary's grief.
The command not to grieve over opponents supplies a direct but differently situated reassurance parallel.
The Prophet's near self-destruction in grief is a distant contrast to Mary's command not to grieve.
The Spirit's appearance to Mary begins the direct encounter whose later childbirth crisis receives this reassurance.
Mary's appeal for refuge to the Merciful establishes the fear and vulnerability preceding divine consolation.
Mary's return carrying the child continues the narrative after the stream, food, drink, and silence instructions.
The accusation against Mary explains the human threat behind the isolation and later instruction not to speak.
Mary's gesture toward the infant directly follows the silence instruction and prepares the issue of who can speak in her place.
Jesus' speech from the cradle is decisive later evidence for a speaking infant in the same birth narrative.
Moses is restored to his mother so her eye is comforted and she does not grieve, an especially close maternal parallel.
Mary's guarded chastity, conception by divine Spirit, and status as a sign give a compact parallel account of the miracle behind 19:24.
The promise that the greatest terror will not grieve the protected gives a broader divine assurance counterpart.
Mary and her son are placed on a secure high ground with a flowing spring, a direct parallel of their divinely provided water and refuge.
The Prophet is told neither to grieve nor be distressed by plotting, another direct reassurance formula.
The absence of grief in Paradise is a distant outcome parallel to Mary's immediate relief from sorrow.
The hardship of a mother bearing and delivering a child supplies relevant embodied context for Mary's labor and need.
The instruction not to grieve over what escapes one offers a general discipline of sorrow relevant to the command to Mary.
Mary's chastity and divine breath are recalled as the basis of Jesus' miraculous birth, directly contextualizing the scene.
God finding the recipient in need and making him self-sufficient offers a compact parallel of merciful provision after vulnerability.
